questions.stem: Which hormone drives the development of female secondary sexual characteristics?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Testosterone drives the male pattern.
Progesterone maintains the uterine lining; it is not the puberty driver.
Insulin manages blood glucose, not puberty.

questions.stem: Which change belongs to the testosterone-driven male list?

options.explanation: Breast development is a female characteristic.

options.text: The voice breaks and the testes start producing sperm
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Widening hips is an oestrogen-driven female change.
Menstruation is female, under the ovarian hormones.

questions.stem: Which changes appear in both males and females at puberty?

options.explanation: The voice break is male-specific.
Menstruation is female-only.

options.text: Both sexes grow the sexual organs and gain body hair
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Hip widening is female-specific.

questions.stem: Why do mood swings and new interest in sex appear during puberty?

options.explanation: School difficulty is not a hormonal cause.

options.text: Because body hair irritates the skin
options.explanation: Irritation does not drive emotional change.
Sleep demand is not the taught cause.

options.text: Because the rising hormone levels also affect the brain and emotions
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A teenager's voice breaks and facial hair appears. Which hormone is responsible, and what broader process is under way?

options.text: Testosterone, as part of male secondary sexual characteristic development
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Oestrogen, as part of the female pattern
options.explanation: The listed changes are male ones.

options.text: Adrenaline, as part of stress response
options.explanation: Adrenaline handles fight-or-flight, not puberty.

options.text: FSH, as part of egg maturation
options.explanation: FSH matures follicles; it is not the voice driver.

questions.stem: State the hormone responsible for male secondary sexual characteristics.
questions.modelAnswer: Testosterone controls the development of male secondary sexual characteristics.

questions.stem: List three female secondary sexual characteristics driven by oestrogen.
questions.modelAnswer: Breasts develop, body hair appears, the menstrual cycle starts and the hips widen.

questions.stem: Explain why body hair growth cannot be used to decide whether oestrogen or testosterone is acting.
questions.modelAnswer: Body hair grows in both sexes during puberty, so it is a shared hormonal change rather than a marker of one sex's hormone.

questions.stem: A clinic charts a patient's puberty progress. State one male-only change, one female-only change and one shared change it would record.
questions.modelAnswer: A male-only change is a breaking voice, a female-only change is the start of the menstrual cycle, and a shared change is the growth of body hair.
